opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, honestly. When I started Taichi during my PhD at MIT, physical simulation was the thing I cared about most. I was working on things like the material point method, fluids, elastic objects, and I kept running into the same problem: writing high-performance simulation code was incredibly painful. You'd have a nice idea on paper, and then spend weeks fighting with CUDA, memory layouts, and sparse data structures before you could even see whether the idea worked.

So the original focus on simulation was very natural. It came from my own pain. And I think that focus was actually a strength early on, because it gave the language a very clear identity. Taichi was designed around things simulation people need: sparse spatial data structures, differentiable programming, easy parallelism over particles and grids. If we had tried to be a general-purpose everything-language from day one, I don't think it would have been nearly as good at anything.

But over time I've also realized that the impact I hope for is bigger than just the simulation community. Simulation researchers are a relatively small group. What I really care about is lowering the barrier to high-performance parallel computing in general, letting someone who has a creative idea in graphics, in visual effects, in robotics, even in education, express it in a few dozen lines of Python-like code and have it run fast on a GPU.

So there's a bit of a tension there. Physical simulation is our root, it's where we have the deepest expertise, and it's a great showcase, because when people see a fluid or a jelly-like object simulated in real time with very little code, they immediately get what Taichi can do. At the same time, if we only stayed there, the ceiling of our impact would be limited. So the way I think about it now is: simulation is the core use case that keeps us honest about performance and productivity, but the infrastructure underneath, the compiler and the runtime, should be general enough to serve a much broader set of people who need parallel computing but don't want to become GPU experts.

In the end, I'd say the simulation focus was the right starting point, but not the final destination. The real goal is to make computational creativity accessible to many more people.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I've gone back and forth on a lot, because when we started Taichi at MIT, physical simulation was both the motivation and the constraint. I was a graphics PhD student. I wanted to simulate snow, sand, elastic materials, fluids, and I was frustrated that writing a high-performance MPM solver meant spending weeks on memory layout, sparse data structures, and GPU kernels before you could even look at a result. So the domain-specific focus wasn't a marketing choice. It was the pain I personally had.

Looking back, I think that focus was exactly right for the early years, and I'd defend it strongly. A general-purpose "fast Python" is an enormous, almost unbounded problem. If we had set out to make all of Python fast, we would have built something mediocre at everything. By saying "we care about spatially sparse, data-oriented, massively parallel computation on grids and particles," we could make real design decisions. Decoupling data structures from computation, the hierarchical sparse layouts, differentiable simulation with DiffTaichi, all of those came directly out of asking what simulation people actually need. A narrow, real user base keeps you honest.

The tension is that if you measure impact by the number of people whose lives are touched, physical simulation looks like a small audience. Graphics researchers, a few hundred labs, some VFX studios. And I'll be honest, there were moments where I worried we had built a beautiful tool for a tiny room.

But I've come to see it differently. First, simulation is upstream of a lot of things people do care about. Robotics, autonomous driving, materials, biomedical modeling, scientific computing broadly. Being the compiler that makes those simulations fast and differentiable is leverage, even if the end user never types "ti.kernel." Second, the thing we actually built turned out to be more general than the label. Once you have a good model for parallel loops over structured and sparse data with Python ergonomics, people start using it for image processing, numerical methods, even procedural art. We've seen that happen organically. I didn't plan for it, and that tells me the abstraction is sound.

So my assessment is: the simulation focus was the right beachhead, and I'd be cautious about anyone who says they would have skipped it. What I'd change is how early we started thinking about the broader audience's experience, documentation, installation, the boring parts. The impact ceiling isn't set by the domain we started in. It's set by whether a scientist who has never written CUDA can get a result in an afternoon. If we do that well, the simulation roots become a strength rather than a limitation.

astra-6.text:
I think physical simulation is a very good starting point, but the impact we hope to have is broader. Simulation is computationally demanding, so it gives us a concrete problem: how do we let people express an idea simply and still run it efficiently on parallel hardware? If we can lower that barrier, more people can experiment without having to become experts in low-level optimization.

So I would assess the focus by whether it helps us build something useful beyond a narrow set of simulations. Physical simulation gives us direction, while the broader goal is to make high-performance programming more accessible.

But the impact I hope we can have is broader: making high-performance computing accessible to more people. If researchers and developers can express an idea in a small amount of code and run it efficiently, they can spend more time exploring ideas and less time optimizing the implementation. So I see physical simulation as a way to build and demonstrate that capability, with the potential to help in other computational fields as well.
